'''Har Gobind Khorana''' (9 January 1922 – 9 November 2011) was an [[Indian Americans|Indian-American]] [[biochemist]].<ref name=NobelBio/> While on the faculty of the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]], he shared the 1968 [[Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine]] with [[Marshall W. Nirenberg]] and [[Robert W. Holley]] for research that showed the order of [[nucleotides]] in [[nucleic acids]], which carry the [[genetic code]] of the cell and control the cell's synthesis of proteins. Khorana and Nirenberg were also awarded the [[Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize]] from [[Columbia University]] in the same year.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cumc.columbia.edu/horwitz |title=The Official Site of Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize |date=14 June 2018 |access-date=16 September 2007 |archive-date=16 October 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131016205105/http://www.cumc.columbia.edu/horwitz/ |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="PLoSBio">{{Cite journal| title=Har Gobind Khorana (1922–2011): Pioneering Spirit |last=Sakmar |first=Thomas P. |date=2012-12-02 |journal=PLOS Biology |volume=10 |issue=2 |article-number=e1001273|language=en-US |issn=1545-7885 |doi=10.1371/journal.pbio.1001273 |pmc=3283548 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Born in [[Raipur, Pakistan|Raipur]], [[Punjab Province (British India)|Punjab]] (during the [[British Raj]]), Khorana served on the faculties of three universities in [[North America]]. He became a [[naturalized citizen]] of the [[United States]] in 1966,<ref name="brit">{{cite encyclopedia |url=https://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/316846/Har-Gobind-Khorana |title=Har Gobind Khorana: American biochemist |encyclopedia=Encyclopaedia Britannica |access-date=21 June 2022 |archive-date=26 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150426084513/http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/316846/Har-Gobind-Khorana| url-status=live}}</ref> and received the [[National Medal of Science]] in 1987.<ref>{{cite web |last=Molina |first=Brett |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/tech/talkingtech/2018/01/09/google-doodle-honors-dna-researcher-har-gobind-khorana/1016000001/ |title=Google Doodle honors DNA researcher Har Gobind Khorana |website=usatoday.com |access-date=9 January 2018 |archive-date=9 January 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180109163857/https://www.usatoday.com/story/tech/talkingtech/2018/01/09/google-doodle-honors-dna-researcher-har-gobind-khorana/1016000001/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

==Biography==
Har Gobind Khorana was born during the [[British Raj]] to Ganpatrai Khorana and Krishna Devi, in [[Raipur, Pakistan|Raipur]], a village near [[Multan]], [[Punjab region|Punjab]], British India, in a [[Punjabi Hindu]] (arora punjabi family).<ref name="auto">{{cite book |last1=Zhao |first1=Xiaojian |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3AxIAgAAQBAJ&q=early+life+har+gobind+khorana&pg=PA653 |title=Asian Americans: An Encyclopedia of Social, Cultural, Economic, and Political History [3 volumes] |last2=Park |first2=Edward J. W. |date=26 November 2013 |publisher=ABC-CLIO |isbn=978-1-59884-240-1 |access-date=9 January 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230924064533/https://books.google.com/books?id=3AxIAgAAQBAJ&q=early+life+har+gobind+khorana&pg=PA653 |archive-date=24 September 2023 |url-status=live |via=Google Books}}</ref> The exact date of his birth is not certain but he believed that it might have been 9 January 1922;<ref name="telegraph.co.uk">{{cite news |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/science-obituaries/8892230/H-Gobind-Khorana.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220112/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/science-obituaries/8892230/H-Gobind-Khorana.html |archive-date=12 January 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |title=H Gobind Khorana |date=15 November 2011 |access-date=7 January 2019 |work=The Telegraph}}{{cbignore}}</ref> this date was later shown in some documents, and has been widely accepted.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2018/01/har-gobind-khorana-google-honours-today-180108134719847.html |title=Har Gobind Khorana: Why Google honours him today |publisher=Al Jazeera |access-date=9 January 2018|archive-date=7 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200807200017/https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2018/01/har-gobind-khorana-google-honours-today-180108134719847.html |url-status=live}}</ref> He was the youngest of five children. His father was a [[patwari]], a village agricultural taxation clerk in the British Indian government. In his autobiography, Khorana wrote this summary: "Although poor, my father was dedicated to educating his children and we were practically the only literate family in the village inhabited by about 100 people."<ref name="mit.edu">{{cite web |last=Finn |first=Emily |url=https://news.mit.edu/2011/obit-khorana-1110 |title=Gobind Khorana, MIT professor emeritus, dies at 89|website=mit.edu |date=11 November 2011 |access-date=9 January 2018 |archive-date=28 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200828040140/https://news.mit.edu/2011/obit-khorana-1110 |url-status=live}}</ref> The first four years of his education were provided under a tree, a spot that was, in effect, the only school in the village."<ref name="auto" />  He did not even own a pencil until age 6.<ref name="Sarkar" />

He attended D.A.V. ([[Dayanand Anglo Vedic|Dayanand Anglo-Vedic]]) High School in [[Multan]] and [[Government College, Lahore|Government College]], in [[Lahore]].<ref name="auto" /> Later, he studied at the [[University of the Punjab|Punjab University]] in [[Lahore]], with the assistance of scholarships, where he obtained a bachelor's degree in 1943<ref name="mit.edu" /> and a Master of Science degree in 1945.<ref name=NobelBio>{{cite web |last1=Kumar |first1=Chandan |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/medicine/laureates/1968/khorana-bio.html |title=H. Gobind Khorana – Biographical |website=Nobel Prize.org |publisher=Nobel Prize |access-date=9 January 2018 |archive-date=12 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180612143416/https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/medicine/laureates/1968/khorana-bio.html |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="independent.co.uk">{{cite web |last=Mindock |first=Clark |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/har-gobind-ghorana-birthday-who-is-he-google-doodle-dna-science-life-career-a8148666.html |title=All you need to know about Har Gobind Ghorana, who Google is celebrating today with a Doodle |date=8 January 2018 |website=Independent |access-date=9 January 2018 |archive-date=8 January 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180108210922/http://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/har-gobind-ghorana-birthday-who-is-he-google-doodle-dna-science-life-career-a8148666.html |url-status=live}}</ref>

Khorana lived in [[British Raj|British ruled India]] until 1945, when he moved to England to study organic chemistry at the [[University of Liverpool]] on a Government of India Fellowship. He received his PhD in 1948 advised by Roger J. S. Beer.<ref name=CenAcs>{{cite web |url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/89/i47/Har-Gobind-Khorana-Dies-89.html |title=Har Gobind Khorana Dies At 89 – November 21, 2011 Issue – Vol. 89 Issue 47 – Chemical & Engineering News |first=Susan J.|last=Ainsworth |website=cen.acs.org |access-date=9 January 2018 |archive-date=1 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200801113157/https://cen.acs.org/articles/89/i47/Har-Gobind-Khorana-Dies-89.html |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Zhao 2014 pp. 652-655">{{cite book |first=Benjamin C. |last=Zulueta |editor-last=Zhao |editor-first=Xiaojian |title=Asian Americans: An Encyclopedia of Social, Cultural, Economic, and Political History |chapter=Khorana, Har Gobind (1922–2011) |publisher=Greenwood, an imprint of ABC-CLIO, LLC |location=Santa Barbara, California |year=2013 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3AxIAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA653 |isbn=978-1-59884-240-1 |pages=652–655 |oclc=911399074 |access-date=6 April 2021 |archive-date=24 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230924064533/https://books.google.com/books?id=3AxIAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA653 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="auto1"/><ref name="mit.edu"/> The following year, he pursued postdoctoral studies with Professor [[Vladimir Prelog]] at [[ETH Zurich]] in [[Switzerland]].<ref name="mit.edu"/> He worked for nearly a year on alkaloid chemistry in an unpaid position.<ref name="auto"/><ref name="auto1">{{cite journal |title=Har Gobind Khorana (1922–2011) |first=Uttam L. |last=RajBhandary |date=14 December 2011 |journal=Nature|volume=480 |issue=7377 |page=322 |pmid=22170673 |doi=10.1038/480322a |bibcode=2011Natur.480..322R |doi-access=free}}</ref>

His family moved to [[Delhi]] from Multan as refugees during the [[partition of India]] and Khorana was never to visit his place of birth after that.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Khorana |first=Alok A. |date=2022-01-08 |title=Dr Har Gobind Khorana at 100: Re-evaluating a shared heritage |url=https://www.dawn.com/news/1668120 |access-date=2023-08-20 |website=DAWN.COM |language=en |quote=The family had to leave Multan, their home for centuries — as it had been for other Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims. Thanks in part to help from Muslim friends, the family all made it alive crossing over as refugees in Delhi in later 1947. Sadly, Gobind would never see his homeland and his favorite sugarcane fields again — a minor yet real tragedy amidst the tragedy of 12 million dispossessed and a million or more murdered on both sides. |archive-date=8 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220108223328/https://www.dawn.com/news/1668120 |url-status=live }}</ref> During a brief period in 1949, he was unable to find a job in Delhi.<ref name="auto"/> He returned to England on a fellowship to work with [[George Wallace Kenner]] and [[Alexander R. Todd]] on peptides and nucleotides.<ref name="auto1"/>  He stayed in Cambridge from 1950 until 1952.

He moved to [[Vancouver]], [[British Columbia]], with his family in 1952 after accepting a position with the British Columbia Research Council at [[University of British Columbia]].<ref name="mit.edu"/><ref>{{cite web |url=https://biochem.ubc.ca/about/history/ |title=History – Department of Biochemistry |website=biochem.ubc.ca |access-date=9 January 2018 |archive-date=1 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200801113450/https://biochem.ubc.ca/about/history/ |url-status=live}}</ref> Khorana was excited by the prospect of starting his own lab, a colleague later recalled.<ref name="auto"/> His mentor later said that the council had few facilities at the time but gave the researcher "all the freedom in the world".<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=O5jQ-GRTvPUC&q=mahan+singh+professor+researcher+Punjab+university&pg=PA370 |title=Physiology Or Medicine, 1963–1970 |first=Jan |last=Lindsten |date=9 January 1999 |publisher=World Scientific |access-date=9 January 2018 |via=Google Books |isbn=978-981-02-3412-6 |archive-date=24 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230924064533/https://books.google.com/books?id=O5jQ-GRTvPUC&q=mahan+singh+professor+researcher+Punjab+university&pg=PA370 |url-status=live}}</ref> His work in British Columbia was on "nucleic acids and synthesis of many important biomolecules" according to the [[American Chemical Society]].<ref name=CenAcs/>

In 1960 Khorana accepted a position as co-director of the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]]'s Institute for Enzyme Research<ref name=CenAcs/><ref name="news.wisc.edu">{{cite web |last=Mitchell |first=Bob |url=http://news.wisc.edu/biochemist-har-gobind-khorana-whose-uw-work-earned-the-nobel-prize-dies/ |title=Biochemist Har Gobind Khorana, whose UW work earned the Nobel Prize, dies |website=news.wisc.edu |date=11 November 2011 |access-date=2017-01-10 |archive-date=12 January 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170112213508/http://news.wisc.edu/biochemist-har-gobind-khorana-whose-uw-work-earned-the-nobel-prize-dies/ |url-status=live }}</ref> He became a professor of biochemistry in 1962 and was named [[Conrad Elvehjem|Conrad A. Elvehjem]] Professor of Life Sciences in 1964.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kresge |first1=Nicole |last2=Simoni |first2=Robert D. |last3=Hill |first3=Robert L. |date=2009-05-29 |title=Total Synthesis of a Tyrosine Suppressor tRNA: the Work of H. Gobind Khorana |journal=The Journal of Biological Chemistry |volume=284 |issue=22 |pages=e5 |doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(19)82144-0 |issn=0021-9258 |pmc=2685647 |doi-access=free}}</ref> While at Wisconsin, "he helped decipher the mechanisms by which RNA codes for the synthesis of proteins" and "began to work on synthesizing functional genes".<ref name=CenAcs /> During his tenure at this university, he completed the work that led to sharing the Nobel Prize in 1968. The Nobel web site states that it was "for their interpretation of the genetic code and its function in protein synthesis". Har Gobind Khorana's role is stated as follows: he "made important contributions to this field by building different RNA chains with the help of enzymes. Using these enzymes, he was able to produce proteins. The amino acid sequences of these proteins then solved the rest of the puzzle."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/medicine/laureates/1968/khorana-facts.html |title=H. Gobind Khorana – Facts |website=www.nobelprize.org |access-date=9 January 2018 |archive-date=1 June 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170601162054/http://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/medicine/laureates/1968/khorana-facts.html |url-status=live}}</ref>

He became a US citizen in 1966.<ref name="vox.com" /> Beginning in 1970, Khorana was the [[Alfred P. Sloan]] Professor of Biology and Chemistry at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]<ref name="Time" /><ref name="mit.edu" /><ref>{{cite web |url=http://web.mit.edu/chemistry/www/faculty/khorana.html |title=MIT HG Khorana MIT laboratory |access-date=21 July 2006 |archive-date=8 October 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121008002203/http://web.mit.edu/chemistry/www/faculty/khorana.html |url-status=live }}</ref> and later, a member of the Board of Scientific Governors at [[The Scripps Research Institute]]. He retired from MIT in 2007.<ref name="vox.com" />

Har Gobind Khorana married Esther Elizabeth Sibler in 1952. They had met in Switzerland and had three children, Julia Elizabeth, Emily Anne, and Dave Roy.

==Research==
[[RNA|Ribonucleic acid]] (RNA) with two repeating units (UCUCUCU → UCU CUC UCU) produced two alternating [[amino acid]]s. This, combined with the [[Nirenberg and Leder experiment]], showed that UCU genetically codes for [[serine]] and CUC codes for [[leucine]]. RNAs with three repeating units (UACUACUA → UAC UAC UAC, or ACU ACU ACU, or CUA CUA CUA) produced three different strings of amino acids. RNAs with four repeating units including UAG, UAA, or UGA, produced only [[dipeptide]]s and [[tripeptide]]s thus revealing that UAG, UAA, and UGA are [[stop codon]]s.<ref name="nobel"/>

Their [[Nobel Prize|Nobel]] lecture was delivered on 12 December 1968.<ref name="nobel">{{cite web |url=https://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/medicine/laureates/1968/khorana-lecture.html |title=HG Khorana Nobel Lecture |access-date=5 February 2011 |archive-date=3 December 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203032746/http://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/medicine/laureates/1968/khorana-lecture.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Khorana was the first scientist to chemically synthesize [[oligonucleotide]]s.<ref name="doi10.1126/science.366749">{{cite journal |last1=Khorana |first1=H. G. |author-link=Har Gobind Khorana |title=Total synthesis of a gene |doi=10.1126/science.366749 |journal=Science |volume=203 |issue=4381 |pages=614–625 |year=1979 |pmid=366749 |bibcode=1979Sci...203..614K |url=https://dspace.mit.edu/bitstream/1721.1/104342/1/12045_2012_Article_134.pdf |access-date=21 September 2019 |archive-date=24 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230924064534/http://dspace.mit.edu/bitstream/handle/1721.1/104342/12045_2012_Article_134.pdf;jsessionid=EF90136887A59CF5EA5F8A62D5A71E3B?sequence=1 |url-status=live }}</ref> This achievement, in the 1970s, was also the world's first synthetic gene; in later years, the process has become widespread.<ref name="Time">{{cite magazine |last=Calfas |first=Jennifer |url=https://time.com/5094695/google-doodle-har-gobind-khorana/ |title=Who Is Har Gobind Khorana? Why Google Is Celebrating the Nobel Prize-Winner |magazine=Time |access-date=9 January 2018 |archive-date=11 January 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180111181608/http://time.com/5094695/google-doodle-har-gobind-khorana/ |url-status=live}}</ref> Subsequent scientists referred to his research while advancing genome editing with the CRISPR/Cas9 system.<ref name="vox.com">{{cite web |last=Irfan |first=Umair |url=https://www.vox.com/2018/1/9/16862980/google-doodle-har-gobind-khorana-genetics-dna |title=Har Gobind Khorana deciphered DNA and wrote the dictionary for our genetic language |website=vox.com |access-date=9 January 2018 |date=9 January 2018 |archive-date=9 January 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180109064607/https://www.vox.com/2018/1/9/16862980/google-doodle-har-gobind-khorana-genetics-dna |url-status=live}}</ref>

===Subsequent research===
After years of work, he was the first in the world to complete the total synthesis of a functional gene outside a living organism in 1972.<ref name="Sarkar">{{cite news |last1=Sarkar |first1=Sahotra |title=Har Gobind Khorana: The chemist who cracked DNA's code and made the first artificial gene was born into poverty 100 years ago in an Indian village |url=https://theconversation.com/har-gobind-khorana-the-chemist-who-cracked-dnas-code-and-made-the-first-artificial-gene-was-born-into-poverty-100-years-ago-in-an-indian-village-178390 |access-date=7 April 2022 |work=The Conversation |date=5 April 2022 |archive-date=6 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220406114055/https://theconversation.com/har-gobind-khorana-the-chemist-who-cracked-dnas-code-and-made-the-first-artificial-gene-was-born-into-poverty-100-years-ago-in-an-indian-village-178390 |url-status=live }}</ref> He did this by extending the above to long DNA polymers using non-aqueous chemistry and assembled these into the first synthetic gene, using [[polymerase]] and [[ligase]] enzymes that link pieces of DNA together,<ref name="doi10.1126/science.366749"/> as well as methods that anticipated the invention of [[polymerase chain reaction]] (PCR).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kleppe |first1=K. |last2=Ohtsuka |first2=E. |last3=Kleppe |first3=R. |last4=Molineux |first4=I. |last5=Khorana |first5=H. G. |author-link5=Har Gobind Khorana |title=Studies on polynucleotides *1, *2XCVI. Repair replication of short synthetic DNA's as catalyzed by DNA polymerases |doi=10.1016/0022-2836(71)90469-4 |journal=Journal of Molecular Biology |volume=56 |issue=2 |pages=341–361 |year=1971 |pmid=4927950 }}</ref>  These custom-designed pieces of artificial genes are widely used in biology labs for sequencing, [[cloning]] and engineering new plants and animals, and are integral to the expanding use of DNA analysis to understand gene-based human disease as well as human evolution. Khorana's invention(s) have become automated and commercialized so that anyone now can order a synthetic [[Oligonucleotide synthesis|oligonucleotide]] or a gene from any of a number of companies. One merely needs to send the [[genetic sequence]] to one of the companies to receive an oligonucleotide with the desired sequence.

After the middle of the 1970s, his lab studied the biochemistry of [[bacteriorhodopsin]], a membrane protein that converts light energy into chemical energy by creating a proton gradient.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wildenauer |first1=D. |last2=Khorana |first2=H. G. |author-link2=Har Gobind Khorana |title=The preparation of lipid-depleted bacteriorhodopsin |journal=Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - Biomembranes |volume=466 |issue=2 |pages=315–324 |year=1977 |pmid=857886 |doi=10.1016/0005-2736(77)90227-9}}</ref> Later, his lab went on to study the structurally related visual pigment known as [[rhodopsin]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ahuja |first1=S. |last2=Crocker |first2=E. |last3=Eilers |first3=M. |last4=Hornak |first4=V. |last5=Hirshfeld |first5=A. |last6=Ziliox |first6=M. |last7=Syrett |first7=N. |last8=Reeves |first8=P. J. |last9=Khorana |first9=H. G. |author-link9=Har Gobind Khorana |last10=Sheves |doi=10.1074/jbc.M805725200 |first10=M. |last11=Smith |first11=S. O. |title=Location of the Retinal Chromophore in the Activated State of Rhodopsin* |journal=Journal of Biological Chemistry |volume=284 |issue=15 |pages=10190–10201 |year=2009 |pmid=19176531 |pmc=2665073|doi-access=free }}</ref>

A summary of his work was provided by a former colleague at the University of Wisconsin: "Khorana was an early practitioner, and perhaps a founding father, of the field of chemical biology. He brought the power of chemical synthesis to bear on deciphering the genetic code, relying on different combinations of trinucleotides."<ref name=CenAcs/><ref name=NobelBio/>

==Awards and honors==
[[File:Har Gobind Khorana receives NIH lecture award.jpg|thumb|Har Gobind Khorana receiving NIH lecture award]]

In addition to sharing the [[Nobel Prize]],<ref name="independent.co.uk"/> Khorana was elected a member of the United States [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1966,<ref>{{Cite web |title=H. Gobind Khorana |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/h-gobind-khorana-ebjqdy/ |access-date=2022-08-11 |website=www.nasonline.org |archive-date=11 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220811142853/http://www.nasonline.org/member-directory/deceased-members/53832.html |url-status=live }}</ref> a member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1967,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Har Gobind Khorana |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/har-gobind-khorana |access-date=2022-08-11 |website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences |language=en |archive-date=11 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220811142853/https://www.amacad.org/person/har-gobind-khorana |url-status=live }}</ref> a member of the [[American Philosophical Society]] in 1973,<ref>{{Cite web |title=APS Member History |url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Khorana&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced |access-date=2022-08-11 |website=search.amphilsoc.org |archive-date=11 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220811142853/https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Khorana&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced |url-status=live }}</ref> and a [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 1978|Foreign Member of the Royal Society (ForMemRS) in 1978]].<ref name="fellows">{{cite web |title=Fellowship of the Royal Society 1660–2015 |url=https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1RVVZY00MZNrK2YCTTzVrbTFH2t3RxoAZah128gQR-NM/pubhtml |publisher=[[Royal Society]] |location=London |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151015185820/https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1RVVZY00MZNrK2YCTTzVrbTFH2t3RxoAZah128gQR-NM/pubhtml |archive-date=15 October 2015 }}</ref> The Indian government awarded Khorana the [[Padma Vibhushan]] in 1969.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Staff |first=The Wire |date=2022-01-09 |title=Remembering Biochemist Har Gobind Khorana on His 100th Birth Anniversary – The Wire Science |url=https://science.thewire.in/society/history/remembering-biochemist-har-gobind-khorana-on-his-100th-birth-anniversary/ |access-date=2023-09-28 |language=en-GB}}</ref>

In 2009, Khorana was hosted by the Khorana Program and honored at the 33rd Steenbock Symposium in [[Madison, Wisconsin]].<ref name="news.wisc.edu"/>

Other honors included the Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize from [[Columbia University]] and the Lasker Foundation Award for Basic Medical Research, both in 1969, the Golden Plate Award of the [[Academy of Achievement|American Academy of Achievement]] in 1971,<ref>{{cite web|title=Golden Plate Awardees of the American Academy of Achievement|website=www.achievement.org|publisher=[[American Academy of Achievement]]|url=https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#science-exploration|access-date=17 May 2020|archive-date=15 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161215023909/https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#science-exploration|url-status=live}}</ref> the Willard Gibbs Medal of the Chicago section of the American Chemical Society, in 1974, the Gairdner Foundation Annual Award, in 1980 and the Paul Kayser International Award of Merit in Retina Research, in 1987.<ref name="mit.edu"/>

On 9 January 2018, a [[Google Doodle]] celebrated the achievements<ref>{{cite web |url=https://doodles.google/doodle/har-gobind-khoranas-96th-birthday/|title=Har Gobind Khorana's 96th Birthday |website=www.google.com |access-date=8 January 2018 |archive-date=8 January 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180108235959/https://www.google.com/doodles/har-gobind-khoranas-96th-birthday |url-status=live}}</ref> of Har Gobind Khorana on what would have been his 96th birthday.<ref name="Google 2018">{{cite web | title=Har Gobind Khorana's 96th Birthday | website=Google | date=2018-01-09 | url=https://doodles.google/doodle/har-gobind-khoranas-96th-birthday/ | access-date=2018-01-10 | archive-date=8 January 2018 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180108235959/https://www.google.com/doodles/har-gobind-khoranas-96th-birthday | url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/tech/talkingtech/2018/01/09/google-doodle-honors-dna-researcher-har-gobind-khorana/1016000001/ |title=Google Doodle honors DNA researcher Har Gobind Khorana |first=Brett |last=Molina |publisher=USA Today |access-date=9 January 2018 |archive-date=9 January 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180109163857/https://www.usatoday.com/story/tech/talkingtech/2018/01/09/google-doodle-honors-dna-researcher-har-gobind-khorana/1016000001/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

The "Khorana Program" by Government of India's [[Department of Biotechnology]], the University of Wisconsin–Madison, Wisconsin–India Science and Technology Exchange Program (WINStep Forward/WSF) and the Indo-US Science and Technology Forum is a scholarship instituted in his name, since 2007 it has offered Indian students research opportunities at certain US universities.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Khorana Program {{!}} WINStep Forward {{!}} Connecting India and the U.S. |url=https://www.winstepforward.org/khorana-program/ |access-date=2023-08-20 |website=WINStep Forward |language=en-US |archive-date=20 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230820181756/https://www.winstepforward.org/khorana-program/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The mission of the Khorana Program is to build a seamless community of scientists, industrialists, and social entrepreneurs in the United States and India. The program is focused on three objectives:<ref>{{cite web |url=http://iusstf.org/story/53-50-Khorana-Program.html |title=Khorana Program for Scholars |website=iusstf.org |publisher=Indo-US Science and Technology Forum |location=New Delhi, India |access-date=2018-01-09 |archive-date=9 January 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180109235508/http://iusstf.org/story/53-50-Khorana-Program.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Providing graduate and undergraduate students with a transformative research experience, engaging partners in rural development and food security, and facilitating public-private partnerships between the U.S. and India. The  WINStep Forward adopted administration responsibilities for the Khorana program in 2007.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.winstepforward.org/history/ |title=History |website=winstepforward.org |publisher=WINStep Forward |location=Madison, WI |access-date=2018-06-26 |archive-date=26 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180626220452/https://www.winstepforward.org/history/ |url-status=live }}</ref> WINStep Forward was jointly created by Drs. Aseem Ansari and [[Ken Shapiro]] at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. WINStep Forward also administers the nationally competitive [[Satyendra Nath Bose|S. N. Bose]] Programs for Indian and American students, respectively, to promote both fundamental and applied research not only in biotechnology but broadly across all STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) fields, including medicine, pharmacy, agriculture, wildlife and climate change.

A park in the Wesbrook Village in the [[University of British Columbia|UBC]] is named after Khorana.<ref name="UNA report 2008">{{cite web |title=University Neighbourhoods Association, Annual Report (September 2008) |url=https://bog2.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2010/10/SUB-BG-081118_4.8.pdf#page=12 |date=2008-11-13 |website=bog2.sites.olt.ubc.ca |access-date=2025-07-23 |page=12 (marked as p. 7) |archive-date=18 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240518231433/https://bog2.sites.olt.ubc.ca/files/2010/10/SUB-BG-081118_4.8.pdf#page=12 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="UBC 2020">{{cite web |title=What's In A Name? |website=Live At UBC |date=2020-04-07 |url=https://www.liveatubc.ca/whats-in-a-name/ |access-date=2025-07-23}}</ref>

==Death==
Khorana died on 9 November 2011, in [[Concord, Massachusetts]], at the age of 89. His wife, Esther, and daughter, Emily Anne, had died earlier,<ref name=CenAcs/> but Khorana was survived by his other two children.<ref name="telegraph.co.uk"/> Julia Elizabeth later wrote about her father's work as a professor: "Even while doing all this research, he was always really interested in education, in students and young people."<ref name="mit.edu"/>
